# Gumbiyajātaka (Ja 366)

**ID:** Ja 366
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Gumbiyajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Gumbiya the Ogre

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Gumbiyajātaka* (Ja 366) is a narrative preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the frame story, the Buddha related this past life while residing at Jetavana to admonish a monk who regretted his ordination after being enticed by the charms of a woman; the Buddha compared the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) to sweet honey mixed with deadly poison left on a path by an ogre named Gumbika or Gumbiya [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. 

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was a caravan leader who cautioned his companions never to consume unfamiliar food found along the road without his permission [Cowell 1897]. A predatory *yakkha* named Gumbiya laid out poisoned honey in a forest clearing to trap, kill, and devour unsuspecting travelers [Cowell 1897; Schönberger 2012]. Those travelers who foolishly gave in to greed perished, while the Bodhisatta was able to rescue the obedient members who had merely tasted it by administering an emetic and restorative sweets [Cowell 1897]. The accompanying verses emphasize that sensual desires resemble lethal bait, destroying those who yield to them while leaving the self-restrained unharmed [Cowell 1897].

The Pali text and commentary were edited by V. Fausböll [Fausböll 1883] and translated into English under E. B. Cowell [Cowell 1897]. Modern scholars note this story as part of the Buddhist canonical portrayal of *yakkhas* as terrifying, man-eating demons setting traps in the wilderness [Schönberger 2012]. DharmaNexus detects significant Pali-internal text reuse between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo), alongside minor cross-language alignments with a Tibetan text (*Kāyavākcittāmanasikāra-nāma*, D2272), while SuttaCentral records no curated canonical parallels [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
